clinicalPearls: Fibroepithelial neoplasm defined by a leaf-like (phyllodes) architecture with hypercellular stroma condensing around clefted epithelium.
Graded as benign, borderline or malignant using stromal cellularity, atypia, mitotic rate, stromal overgrowth and the nature of the tumour margin.
Typically presents as a firm, mobile, painless mass that enlarges more rapidly than a fibroadenoma, often in women in their fourth to fifth decade.
Core biopsy cannot reliably distinguish a phyllodes tumour from a cellular fibroadenoma; a report of 'cellular fibroepithelial lesion' warrants excision for definitive classification.
Wide local excision aiming for a clear margin (conventionally around 1 cm) is the mainstay; enucleation predisposes to local recurrence.
Axillary node dissection is not indicated as spread of malignant phyllodes is haematogenous, chiefly to lung and bone, rather than lymphatic.
Malignant transformation is characterised by pure stromal sarcomatous overgrowth; heterologous elements such as liposarcoma may occur.
Recurrence can show progression to a higher grade, so long-term clinical and imaging surveillance is advised after excision.
reference.pathophysiology: Phyllodes tumours are biphasic fibroepithelial neoplasms arising from the intralobular (periductal) hormone-responsive stroma. Unlike fibroadenomas, the stromal component is the neoplastic driver and shows variable hypercellularity, atypia and mitotic activity, producing the characteristic elongated leaf-like fronds lined by benign ductal and myoepithelial epithelium. Progressive accumulation of stromal genetic alterations, including MED12 mutations shared with fibroadenoma and additional changes such as TERT promoter mutations and later cytogenetic aberrations, underlies the spectrum from benign through borderline to frankly malignant lesions in which the stroma overgrows and behaves as a sarcoma.
additionalDifferentials: Fibroadenoma, particularly the cellular or juvenile variant
Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia forming a mass
additionalInvestigations: Triple assessment with clinical examination, ultrasound and mammography
Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy for tissue architecture
Breast MRI to delineate large lesions and plan margins
Definitive excisional histology with margin assessment and grading
Immunohistochemistry (CD34, beta-catenin, p53, Ki-67) to support classification
Staging chest imaging where malignant phyllodes is confirmed
Multidisciplinary review of borderline and malignant cases
redFlags: Rapid interval enlargement of a previously stable breast mass
Very large tumour with overlying skin stretching, ulceration or venous prominence
Histological stromal overgrowth with high mitotic count and infiltrative margin
New respiratory or skeletal symptoms suggesting haematogenous metastasis
Repeated local recurrence with rising histological grade
reference.prognosis: Benign phyllodes tumours have an excellent outlook after complete excision, though local recurrence may occur if margins are inadequate. Borderline and malignant lesions carry progressively higher recurrence and, for malignant tumours, a meaningful risk of distant metastasis that markedly worsens survival.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a phyllodes tumour as a fibroadenoma on core biopsy and undertreating with simple enucleation
Performing unnecessary axillary surgery, since spread is haematogenous rather than nodal
Failing to obtain an adequate margin, the principal driver of local recurrence
Assuming benign histology excludes recurrence and omitting follow-up surveillance
Overlooking sarcomatous heterologous elements that upgrade a lesion to malignant

management: Perform wide local excision aiming for a clear margin as definitive treatment, with mastectomy for large lesions relative to breast size
Avoid enucleation, which leaves positive margins and predisposes to recurrence, and re-excise when margins are inadequate
Do not undertake axillary dissection, as malignant tumours metastasise haematogenously to lung and bone rather than to nodes
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy for malignant and selected borderline tumours or after re-excision
Reserve systemic sarcoma-type chemotherapy for large malignant or metastatic disease
Follow up with clinical examination and breast imaging for local recurrence, and stage the chest when malignant phyllodes is confirmed
Manage through a breast multidisciplinary team with specialist histological grading
